articles.sourceTitle: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE in PHP
articles.title: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
articles.text: Executive SummaryWiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them. PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it, putting every affected website in immediate risk. Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine. These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability  required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.OverviewIn this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Google, Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel, and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.The VulnerabilitiesAll of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.Below you can find a table that demonstrates what type of impact was demonstrated by each of the bugs we reported to PHP. The applications listed below are targets we chose for the RCE demonstrations. They are representative targets - exploitation does not require one of these CMSs, as the vulnerable code is in PHP itself.While this blog covers only four instances of exploitable bugs (grouped under two CVEs) that follow this problematic pattern, there are other tracked, and likely untracked, variants of this issue in the PHP codebase. These variants have different requirements for exploitation and can lead to different types of impact. In any case, the patch provided by the PHP team fixes the issue at its core and eliminates all variants in the patched release.ImpactWe combined these vulnerabilities into a single exploit script, php2shell, and demonstrated that it could execute code remotely without authentication on deployments of WordPress (wordpress:latest), Drupal (drupal:latest), and Joomla (joomla:latest), using their latest container images at the time of testing.These platforms illustrate the impact, but the vulnerabilities are in PHP itself. Exploitation does not depend on a flaw in the application’s code: even a simple “Hello World” application running on an affected PHP version can be vulnerable.Separately, we demonstrated that attackers could read sensitive data from the PHP process’s memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys, without needing to achieve remote code execution.Demonstrations of PHP2Shell with Wordpress, Joomla, and Drupal: The AI inflection pointThe vulnerable code had been present for more than a decade. Turning these flaws into working exploits required chaining multiple bugs and accounting for how PHP allocates and reuses memory across requests. Memory bugs are notoriously complex; differences in PHP versions, configurations and application behavior can break assumptions the exploit depends on. An attack that works against one deployment may need substantial adjustments to work against another, each requiring further analysis, testing and debugging. Pre-AI, this manual work would be difficult to implement and even harder to scale. With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts. With testing and debugging tools, models can analyze failures and iterate on adjustments, reducing the specialist effort required for each target. This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments.This changes the economics of both discovery and exploitation. As AI reduces the effort needed to develop and adapt complex exploits, vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets. We used Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol throughout this research. Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.Using Gemini 4 Argon, the team at Wiz has shown why frontier AI is a game-changer for cyber defense. For over a decade, these critical vulnerabilities remained unaddressed because vulnerability discovery and exploitation were incredibly complex. We're pleased to see Gemini 4 Argon help defenders bridge that gap, finding vulnerabilities and helping patch them.Raluca Ada Popa, Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMindIndustry-level collaborationsPrior to public disclosure, Wiz Research worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI on discovery, coordination and patch verification. We also partnered with Google Cloud, Cloudflare, AWS, Microsoft, Automattic, Fastly, Akamai, Imperva, Vercel and many others to prepare customer guidance, detections and out-of-the-box mitigations for organizations that cannot update immediately.A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application. PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.Technical deep diveBug: Upload-progress unserializer use-after-freePHP's Session module can decode session data during upload-progress handling in the same pre-initialization window. The decoder stores request-owned bookkeeping in BG(unserialize). A fatal allocation failure can interrupt this path, destroy the request heap and leave the unserializer's global state published.On a later request handled by the same worker, PHP can consume attacker-reclaimed memory as live unserializer bookkeeping. The stale state becomes a powerful memory-corruption primitive. We combined it with the memory disclosure to remove address uncertainty and achieved unauthenticated remote code execution on WordPress, Drupal and Joomla.The WordPress, Drupal and Joomla chains are representative demonstrations. The underlying primitives exist at the PHP engine level and can affect any PHP application running on a vulnerable version.These issues execute below the application layer, so application logs may contain little context. Until systems are patched, defenders should pay particular attention to unusual multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses, unexpectedly large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies, and unexplained PHP worker churn. These signals can guide an investigation. Applying the PHP security update remains the only complete remediation.Bug: Remote process-memory disclosurePHP parses RFC1867 multipart requests during request startup, before normal module initialization has completed. Session upload-progress handling can initialize Session state at this early stage and publish a session ID in PS(id). An out-of-memory error can abort the request before cleanup completes. PHP then destroys the request heap and may leave PS(id) pointing to the freed allocation.A later multipart request handled by the same worker can reach the upload-progress cleanup path before normal Session initialization resets that pointer. PHP trusts the stale pointer and length as a live zend_string and URL-encodes the reclaimed heap contents into a PHPSESSID response cookie. The attack works even when the application never calls session_start(), making the issue application-agnostic. We demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of an attacker-sized region of live worker memory containing data from outside the attacker's request.Bug: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-freeIn affected versions, PHP retains the backtrace of the most recent fatal error in EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). A fatal out-of-memory error can destroy the request heap without undefining that executor-global value. The worker survives with a global that still points to memory from the previous request.If the same worker emits a diagnostic early in the next request, it can access the pointer before the executor reinitializes that state. PHP then destroys or updates the dangling backtrace and follows attacker-reclaimed memory. The resulting cross-request use-after-free can be developed into controlled memory corruption. We demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against Drupal using this primitive.Bug: OPcache type confusionOPcache persists compiled PHP structures in shared memory and assigns indices into per-worker runtime-pointer maps. Workers coordinate those indices through a shared frontier. During zend_accel_script_persist(), PHP advances the process-local CG(map_ptr_

articles.title: Voice Agent SDK & Speech Models in 50+ Languages
articles.text: Voxtral 3 introduces a cutting-edge voice agent SDK and state-of-the-art speech models designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across 50+ languages. It combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration for seamless workflow automation. Available via Mistral’s EU-hosted API or self-deployment, it ensures data sovereignty while delivering low-latency, human-like interactions for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult. A reliable voice agent needs to do four things very well (and simultaneously): Listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,Reason deeply about what users mean in specific contexts,Speak naturally with emotion and expression, and Take action over multiple steps through connected systems. Getting all four to work together reliably in real time remains a challenge. To address this, we introduce Voxtral 3: a new family of state-of-the-art speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, alongside a voice agent SDK that brings listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline.Voxtral 3 is built to create natural conversational experiences, from contact-center agents and service desks to virtual assistants and hands-free copilots. With support for dozens of languages, expressive speech, complex reasoning, and deep integration with your own tools and data, agents built with Voxtral can interpret nuanced intent, reason through sophisticated requests, and execute multi-step actions across connected systems.As with other Mistral models, the Voxtral 3 family is designed for sovereign deployment. Available today through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment on your own infrastructure, it gives organizations control over where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are retained.HighlightsAccurate transcription across 50+ languages. The speech-to-text model, Voxtral Small Transcribe 3, is state-of-the-art in multilingual transcription, identifying who said what (diarization), using keyphrases to improve its accuracy (context-biasing). It detects when someone has finished speaking so agents can respond without delay (end-of-turn detection).Natural speech that adapts to the conversation. The text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, introduces new voices that adjust their emotion, pace, and emphasis based on conversational context, with support for 35+ languages and 50+ dialects.Human-like intelligence at your (spoken) command. The new voice agent SDK combines listening, reasoning, tool calling, and speaking into a real-time experience. Agents can retrieve information, interact with business systems, and complete tasks during live conversations over phone or web.Pro Voice for distinctly accurate voice adaptation. For professional use cases where basic voice cloning does not suffice, Voxtral’s Pro Voice adaptation is able to reproduce a speaker’s distinctive character, emotional range, and speaking style across languages, using just 30 minutes of audio. Your voice AI, on your infrastructure. Use Mistral's EU-hosted API or deploy Voxtral 3 on your own infrastructure. Keep sensitive conversations within your environment and control whether any audio is retained. Try Voxtral now  | Learn moreIt hears 50+ languages, with state-of-the-art accuracy.Voxtral Transcribe 3 represents a significant milestone across transcription, diarization (who spoke when) and context biasing capabilities. The supported list of languages is expanded to 50, including 24 official EU languages and many low-resource Asian and Indic languages.The Small version achieves state-of-the-art results across diarization and multilingual transcription, including in English, French and Spanish. It outperforms Whisper, Scribe v2 and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. The Mini variant is 4B parameters, enabling fast and accurate transcriptions at a price of $0.0035/min.Both models support context biasing, where key terms and free-form text can be given to bias the transcription and improve recall on technical terms. articles.sourceTitle: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
articles.title: deepseek-ai/DeepInfer: DeepInfer: High-performance, large-scale inference framework for DeepSeek models · GitHub
articles.text:
DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale.
Supported models:

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Supported features:

Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime
Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB
DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification
SWA bounded replay
Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler)
Batch-invariant inference
Deterministic sampling
Structured outputs

Feature details and configuration

Optimized kernels: FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, TileKernels, DeepSelect, and custom TileLang kernels.
DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5).
Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length.
Asynchronous scheduling: overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default.
Batch-invariant inference: keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA only).
Deterministic sampling: produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 and pass a fixed seq_seed to SamplingParams (NVIDIA only).
Structured outputs: constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...} to SamplingParams; see examples.

Supported hardware:

NVIDIA SM100 GPUs
Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs

Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release):

A KV cache system
VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented)
Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode

Linux
GCC >= 13.0
Python 3.12
CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only)
CANN 9.2 (Ascend only)

Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment.
# Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform
# Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer
export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia
./build.sh

The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, is
downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to
run from a local copy instead.
python examples/offline_inference.py
See examples for details.

Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see run_sweep.sh.

See eval/README.md.

DeepInfer is released under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details.

DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. We thank their developers.

articles.sourceTitle: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
articles.title: Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web
articles.text: What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT...About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake.Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research.At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore. Where the idea for publishing fake statistics came fromThe impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds).In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for.Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website.I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published an eye-opening study in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas.The setup: a website and 50,000 made-up stats, created in one dayQuick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment:I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50.The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in Growth Memo, it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results.What happenedGoogle buried the site almost immediatelyWhen I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results.Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed.I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help.Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know.But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months.In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question.Unlike Google, ChatGPT never stopped pulling from the siteAnd when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT really never stopped.After 7 months, the site now has 330+ referring domainsAccording to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better.ChatGPT is still citing it to this dayGoogle may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch.If you've read Tomek's ChatGPT Index research, you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long. A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval.I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory!Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, stateglobe.com was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista.Retrieval is not rankingThe constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems.When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps.StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back.For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.”Fake data turned into real citationsYou’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right. StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was……cited in an academic paper……used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group……cited by an economics publication in India……and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community.Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link.The uncomfortable implication: citation launderingOn day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain.Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions.The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy.It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows."This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows.Lastly, we tried running our experiment with real dataOnce I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics.Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality.Lessons learnedWhy publishing statistics leads to LLM citationsThe two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple:More and more content is written with LLMs.When an LLM writes, it researches the appropriate topic.When the LLM hits a gap, it looks for a number to fill it.The reasons behind this process are equally clear.Research means fanout queries asking for statisticsWhen a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results.A number looks like evidence that can fill knowledge gapsWhen a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t.The model doesn’t check the numberA search-grounded piece of LLM-written content has a tight budget for latency and cost. The system fetches a few pages, pulls the relevant passages, and starts to write. Fact-checking doesn’t happen anywhere in the process.Verifying a single statistic would mean finding independent sources, comparing them, and resolving conflicts. Across billions of prompts by millions of users, the costs in both time and money would add up, making verification too slow and too expensive for practical purposes.To get around this, LLMs use rerankers that score relevance, but not truth. That means if a passage matches the query and looks authoritative, it gets used.Statistics have a built-in freshness that models likeI've written before about ChatGPT's recency bias in how it scores sources. Statistics pages contain the year in the title, the headings, and the URL. Three built-in signals to the model that what’s on the page is fresh.How to build a statistics page the right wayThe two tests I ran show that statistics pages are a very powerful way to get your content cited by LLMs. While I absolutely do not recommend coming up with bogus data, you can use the learnings from our small test to create your own pages with real data. Here's what worked for us at Peec and what I would do if I were making a statistics page again.Make one claim per sentence. Each stat should make sense on its own, out of context. Retrieval doesn’t work on pages, but rather on passages. If a number needs the paragraph above it to make sense, it probably won't get pulled.Put the source and year next to every number. "According to [Source] (2026), X%..." This helps the model, the human editor, and your credibility. It’s one small piece of information hygiene that benefits the broader information environment.Match headings to fanout queries.
